title: Behemoth beside the victor; the dragon’s hide and costume
english: … and on the basilisk you will tread (Psalm 91:13).
“But see, there are wild beasts beside you” (Job 40:15).
From the same: Beside you, Job; beside everyone who is mindful; beside everyone who has won the victory.

“He eats grass just like oxen” (Job 40:15). He means the worms, the ones that came out of Job himself and were eating him up. For “an end,” he says, “my hand by you”; and see, it eats him up like grass.
“And his power is on the navel of his belly” (Job 40:16). This is the first power set against the man. It is from here that it begins to make him a fornicator.

From the same: This is said to signify the female, to show that it wages war not only against those who carry the seed. And most fittingly of all, he named the loin in the case of the male and the navel of the belly in the case of the woman: “See, his strength: his loin is in strength; and his power is on the navel of his belly” (Job 40:16).

“And nations of Phoenicians divide it up” (Job 41:6). Since the Canaanites, who are also the Phoenicians, are charged with great wickedness, that is why he says, “And nations of Phoenicians will divide him up.” Each one takes some part of the dragon, if by race he is a Canaanite and a Phoenician.

“And if every ship came together, they could not carry a single hide of his tail” (Job 41:7). The last parts of the dragon, his very extremities, all the ships together cannot put to death. Human beings, who use their bodies as ships, cannot carry a single hide of his tail. By themselves, on their own, they cannot. But when divine power watches over us, we are able to carry not only a single hide of his tail but the whole of him, and to put the whole of him to death. And each of us puts the devil to death, as far as it lies with himself, in keeping with what is said by the Apostle: “And may God crush Satan under your feet soon” (Romans 16:20).

“Who will uncover the face of his clothing?” (Job 41:13). Why did he not say, “Who will uncover his face?” What is the clothing doing here as well? For “who will uncover,” he says, “the face of his clothing?” So that what is said may be understood, let us use the example of the masks that people put on, who do not appear as what they are but as what they wish to seem. For they take up masks, let us say, …
